\[
r_{1,2} = p \pm (d \cos\theta,\ d \sin\theta),
\quad
r_{3,4} = p \pm (-d \sin\theta,\ d \cos\theta),
\qquad
q(p) = \begin{cases} \tfrac{1}{4} \sum_i I(r_i) & \max_i \lvert I(r_i) - I(p) \rvert < T \\ I(p) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases},
\qquad
d \le 16,\ T = 4
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(p\): The pixel
- \(r_i\): The four reference pixels
- \(d, \theta\): The random distance and angle of pixel p
- \(T\): The threshold

Banding is a gradient drawn with too few levels, so it breaks into flat steps. A flat step has no detail to keep, so it can be replaced by an average over a wide area, which brings back the levels in between. Real edges must be kept. For every pixel p, the filter draws a distance d from 1 to the range and an angle theta, at random but with a fixed seed. The four references are p plus and minus d in that direction, and p plus and minus d at right angles to it, rounded to whole pixels. If all four lie within the threshold T of the pixel, the area is flat or a gentle step, and the pixel takes their mean. Otherwise it stays. The random positions turn the step into fine grain, which the eye accepts better than a sharp contour. This follows the idea of the deband filters of flash3kyuu_deband and FFmpeg. The details here are PixelNexus's own.
